question: What does the Bible say about speaking in tongues?
intro: Acts and 1 Corinthians tell of people who spoke in tongues, and Christians read them differently on three things: whether the gift is still given today, what the speech is (a human language, or speech no human community speaks), and how it belongs in the life of a church. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that people spoke in tongues when the Spirit came upon them at Pentecost, in the house of Cornelius and at Ephesus; that Paul lists tongues among the gifts the Spirit gives for the common good; that in the gathered church tongues are to be interpreted and everything done to build up the church; and that, without love, the one who has these gifts is nothing (13:1-3). The readings differ on whether the gift continues after the apostles' age, and on what the speech is.

passages.quote: And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.
Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.
If I have the gift of prophecy and can fathom all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
All of these must be done to build up the church.

readings.label: The gifts continue: speaking in tongues is a gift the Spirit still gives, for prayer and for the church
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to show tongues given at Pentecost, at Cornelius's house and at Ephesus, and then in the ordinary life of the church at Corinth, and they find nothing in it that sets a date on which the gift ends. They take the promise of Acts 2:39 and the Spirit's apportioning of gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 to reach every generation of believers. Pentecostal and Charismatic churches hold this as part of the Spirit's present work, with tongues used in private prayer (what is often called a prayer language) and in worship with interpretation; the Assemblies of God (Statement of Fundamental Truths 7 and 8) and the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) teach that tongues is the first outward sign of being baptized in the Holy Spirit (what is called initial evidence), which the Assemblies of God teach as an experience distinct from and after the new birth, and other Pentecostal and Charismatic churches do not teach it. On what the speech is, holders differ: some take the tongues of Acts 2 as human languages the speakers had not learned, and many take the tongues of Corinth as speech to God in a language no human community speaks (14:2). Members of other traditions, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist and Methodist members among them, hold this reading in part, especially in charismatic renewal movements within their churches.

passages.quote: This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off-to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.
passages.note: Read as carrying the Spirit's promise past the first hearers, to children and to those far off.

passages.quote: For they heard them speaking in tongues and exalting God.
passages.note: Tongues given again, in another place and to a household of Gentiles.

passages.quote: And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
passages.note: Tongues given again, in Ephesus, as an event that recurs and is not confined to the first day.

passages.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels
passages.note: Read as allowing for speech beyond the languages of men, since Paul names the tongues of angels.

passages.quote: For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God. Indeed, no one understands him; he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
passages.note: Read as describing speech addressed to God, in the Spirit, that the hearers do not understand.

passages.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church.
passages.note: Read as the speaker being built up by the gift, in private prayer.

passages.quote: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
passages.note: Read as naming prayer in a tongue, with the spirit praying.

passages.quote: So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
passages.note: Read as a standing instruction that the gift is not to be forbidden.

passages.quote: to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues
passages.note: Tongues and the interpretation of tongues are named among the gifts the Spirit gives.

passages.quote: I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy.
passages.note: Paul says he wishes all of them spoke in tongues, and that he would rather they prophesy.

passages.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.
passages.note: Paul says that he himself speaks in tongues, more than all of them.

passages.quote: In the last days, God says, I will pour out My Spirit on all people.
passages.note: Peter, quoting Joel, says that in the last days God pours out His Spirit on all people. The verse does not name tongues. Readers who hold this reading take 'the last days' to include the present; others take Peter to mean the day of Pentecost.

passages.quote: these signs will accompany those who believe: In My name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues
passages.note: Speaking in new tongues is listed among the signs that go with those who believe. This verse is in the longer ending of Mark (16:9-20), which some of the earliest manuscripts lack; the site marks that ending.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take “the perfect” of 1 Corinthians 13:10 to be the return of Christ (13:12, “then we shall see face to face”), so that prophecy, tongues and knowledge all last until then. They take 14:22 to name one use of tongues, as a sign to unbelievers, beside the uses 14:2, 14:4 and 14:14 describe: speech to God, building up the speaker, and prayer. They take the rules of 14:27-28 and 14:40 as guidance for using the gift in the gathered church, and not as grounds for forbidding it. They take the different Greek verb said of tongues in 13:8 to be a variation of wording, with all three gifts ending together at “the perfect”.

readings.label: The sign gifts have ended (what is called cessationism): tongues belonged to the apostles' age, as a sign
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the signs that marked the apostles (miracles, healing, tongues) to have been given to confirm the first preaching of the gospel and the founding of the church, and to have ended when that foundation was laid. They take the tongues of Acts 2 as human languages, each hearer hearing his own (2:6, 2:8), and the tongues of Corinth as the same gift, real languages that need an interpreter (14:10-11). Reformed and Baptist or free-church readers hold this, and their members differ over when the gifts ended and over how far the ending reaches, to healing and to prophecy as well as tongues. Among Reformed bodies, the Westminster Confession (the standard of the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church) says that God's former ways of revealing his will have ceased (1.1), and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church's 1978 General Assembly report concludes that prophecy and tongues ceased with the close of the apostolic age. Among Baptists, the General Association of Regular Baptist Churches states in its Articles of Faith that the sign and revelatory gifts have fulfilled their purpose and are not applicable to the work of the Holy Spirit today, and the 1689 London Confession (chapter 1) says that the former ways of God's revealing his will have ceased; the Baptist Faith and Message (Southern Baptist Convention, 2000) says the Spirit bestows gifts for service and does not mention tongues or their ending. Many who hold this reading affirm that the Spirit still works in believers, and that God still heals and answers prayer; what they hold to have ended is the gift of tongues and the other sign gifts. Members of both traditions are also found in the third reading.

passages.quote: each one heard them speaking his own language.
passages.note: Read as tongues being known human languages, given as a sign to the nations gathered at the church's beginning.

passages.quote: All the circumcised believers who had accompanied Peter were astounded that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles.
passages.note: Read as a sign to Jewish believers that the Gentiles were received, at a point where the church was opening to the nations.

passages.quote: And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
passages.note: Read as another point of transition, for disciples who had not heard that there is a Holy Spirit (19:2).

passages.quote: And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles, and those with gifts of healing, helping, administration, and various tongues.
passages.note: Read as setting tongues in a list that begins with the apostles and prophets of the church's foundation.

passages.quote: where there are prophecies, they will cease; where there are tongues, they will be restrained; where there is knowledge, it will be dismissed.
passages.note: Read as naming tongues as something that ends. The site marks that the Greek verb here, which the Berean renders “restrained”, differs from the verb said of prophecies and knowledge; holders of this reading take that difference to say tongues cease of themselves.

passages.quote: but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away.
passages.note: Many holders take “the perfect” as the completed foundation of the church and its scriptures; others in this reading take it differently.

passages.quote: Tongues, then, are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers.
passages.note: Read as tongues being a sign for those outside, a purpose that belongs to the church's opening. The verse before (14:21) has Paul say “It is written in the Law” (the scriptures of Israel) and give the words “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people”; they are taken from Isaiah 28:11-12, where they are addressed to Isaiah's own people, and Paul's wording differs from Isaiah's. Read as foreign speech being a sign to a people who do not listen.
passages.context_note: The same verse goes on: 'Prophecy, however, is for believers, not for unbelievers.' The next verse gives a case: 'So if the whole church comes together and everyone speaks in tongues, and some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?'

passages.quote: and was affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will.
passages.note: Read as signs that affirmed the message at its first preaching.

passages.quote: built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone
passages.note: The household of God is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone.

passages.quote: By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me
passages.note: Paul says it is written in the Law that God will speak to this people by strange tongues and foreign lips, and that even then they will not listen.

passages.quote: And last of all He appeared to me also
passages.note: Paul says that last of all Christ appeared to him also. Read as marking Paul as the last of the apostles.

passages.quote: The marks of a true apostle-signs, wonders, and miracles-were performed among you
passages.note: Paul calls signs, wonders, and miracles the marks of a true apostle, performed among the Corinthians. Read as tying such signs to the apostles.

passages.quote: The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people
passages.note: The apostles perform many signs and wonders among the people. Read as tying such signs to the apostles.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take 1 Corinthians 14:39 and 14:5 as Paul's counsel to the church at Corinth while the gift was given, and take 12:11 (“who apportions them to each one as He determines”) to say that the Spirit gives as He wills, an apportioning they read as having changed with the church's age. They take the promise of Acts 2:39 to be the gift of the Holy Spirit named in 2:38 and not each sign that came with it at Pentecost. They take “the tongues of men and of angels” (13:1) as Paul's exaggeration, in a run of “if I” sayings (13:1-3). They take 14:2 to describe a speech that no one understands because no one has interpreted it, and 14:10-11 to say that every language in the world has meaning.

readings.label: The Spirit may give the gift today, and whatever is practiced is tested, interpreted and ordered
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to say that the Spirit apportions gifts as He determines, that not every believer is given this one, that in the gathered church it needs interpretation and order, and that love comes first. They take the text to leave open whether, and until when, the gift is given, and they leave open whether the speech is a human language or another. Members of Catholic, Anglican, Reformed, Baptist and Wesleyan traditions are found here, each with their own emphasis: Catholic teaching, for example, speaks of the Spirit's gifts as given for the good of the church, to be received with thanksgiving and tested by those who lead it (Catechism 799-801 and 2003; Lumen Gentium 12). The Orthodox Church in America's teaching on prayer in the Spirit does not say the gifts have ended; it speaks of tongues as a gift Paul describes and that some believers have in our time, finds no evidence that the saints prayed in tongues or that it belonged to the church's liturgy, and says it needs interpretation and order. Lutheran teaching, as the commission of the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod stated it in 1972, holds that God does not necessarily give his church in all ages the same special gifts, rejects making tongues the primary or indispensable sign of baptism in the Spirit, teaches no second work of the Spirit beyond conversion, and holds that the Spirit comes through the Word and sacraments; Lutheran members within charismatic renewal differ. The Christian Reformed Church's position statement says Christ distributes his gifts when and where he wills, that genuine gifts may be exercised provided all things are done for edification and in good order, and that they are confirmed by the fruit of the Spirit; the Presbyterian Church in America's pastoral letter does not forbid tongues, rejects them as a means of new revelation or as an essential sign of Spirit baptism, and urges forbearance among those who differ. The Anglican Church in North America's catechism lists tongues and their interpretation among the gifts the Spirit distributes as he wills for the sake of the body of Christ. The United Methodist Church's guidelines on the charismatic movement call on the church to be aware of the Holy Spirit's manifestations today, describe the charismatic movement as stressing Spirit baptism without making tongues its initial evidence, and say that when tongues are spoken in a group there must be interpretation to ensure order. The 1995 Mennonite confession does not name tongues; it says the Spirit gives gifts to each member and still speaks, and that what is claimed is to be tested in the congregation against Christ and the Scriptures. Anabaptist congregations differ among themselves. Baptist members are found here too; the Baptist Faith and Message and the other Baptist documents read do not state this reading. Members of each of these traditions are also found in the first two readings.

passages.quote: All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.
passages.note: The Spirit decides who receives which gift.

passages.quote: Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?
passages.note: Paul's questions are read as expecting that not every believer has this gift.

passages.quote: in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.
passages.note: In the gathered church, understanding comes first.

passages.quote: If anyone speaks in a tongue, two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret.
passages.note: Tongues in the assembly: in turn, with an interpreter.

passages.quote: if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God.
passages.note: Without an interpreter, silence in the church and speech to God.

passages.quote: For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace-as in all the churches of the saints.
passages.note: The ground Paul gives beside the rules for tongues and prophecy.

passages.quote: So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.
passages.note: Read together with 14:40: the gift is not forbidden, and it is practiced in order. The first reading also cites this verse.

passages.quote: everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.
passages.note: Closes the chapter on tongues and prophecy.

passages.quote: the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret
passages.note: The one who speaks in a tongue is told to pray that he may interpret.

passages.quote: strive to excel in gifts that build up the church
passages.note: Paul says the Corinthians are eager to have spiritual gifts, and tells them to strive to excel in gifts that build up the church.

passages.quote: unless he interprets so that the church may be edified
passages.note: The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues unless the latter interprets, so that the church is built up.

passages.quote: the others should weigh carefully what is said
passages.note: Two or three prophets are to speak, and the others weigh what is said.

passages.quote: test all things. Hold fast to what is good.
passages.note: Prophecies are not to be despised; all things are to be tested and what is good held fast.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take 1 Corinthians 13:8-10 to say that tongues end at “the perfect”, and they leave open what the perfect is and when it comes, since the first two readings take it differently. They take Acts 2:39 and 14:39 to keep the gift possible without making it the mark of every believer (12:30). They take the accounts in Acts 2, 10 and 19 as events with their own settings, and not as a pattern fixed for every conversion.

terms.note: The name for the reading that the sign gifts, tongues among them, ended with the apostles' age; those who hold it and those who differ both use the word.
The name for the reading that the gifts continue; the word is used of the first reading, and of the third by those who share its openness.

The Pentecostal and Charismatic phrase for an infilling of the Spirit that the Assemblies of God teach as distinct from and after the new birth, and the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) as following a clean heart; other traditions apply the phrase to conversion itself (1 Corinthians 12:13), and Wesleyan holiness churches to entire sanctification.
The teaching, in some Pentecostal churches, that speaking in tongues is the first outward sign of baptism in the Holy Spirit; other Pentecostal and Charismatic churches do not teach it.
The Pentecostal and Charismatic phrase for tongues used in private prayer, drawing on 1 Corinthians 14:2 and 14:14.

Scholars' words: glossolalia is speech in a tongue not known as any human language, xenolalia speech in a human language the speaker has not learned. Readers differ on which the text describes in Acts and in Corinth.
The Greek word of 1 Corinthians 13:10, rendered “the perfect”; readers differ over whether it means the return of Christ, the completed scriptures, or the full growth of the church.

The Greek word for a gift of the Spirit (charisma, “gifts” in 1 Corinthians 12:28), used across the churches; Catholic teaching uses it of gifts given for the good of the church, and names the gift of tongues among the extraordinary ones (Catechism 2003).

The title of a sermon by John Wesley, in which he gives as the cause of the extraordinary gifts becoming rare that the love of many Christians grew cold, and rejects the account that the gifts were no longer needed. It is a founding writer's sermon and not one of the Methodist doctrinal standards.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 799-801 (The Church: charisms)
further_reading.says: It teaches that charisms, whether extraordinary or simple, are graces of the Holy Spirit for the good of the Church, are to be accepted with gratitude, and are to be submitted to the Church's shepherds, whose task is to test all things.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2003 (Grace and Justification: Grace)
further_reading.says: It names charisms, whether extraordinary, such as the gift of miracles or of tongues, as oriented toward sanctifying grace and intended for the common good of the Church.

further_reading.title: Second Vatican Council, Lumen Gentium (Dogmatic Constitution on the Church), 12
further_reading.says: It teaches that the Spirit distributes special graces among the faithful of every rank, to be received with thanksgiving, that extraordinary gifts are not to be sought after, and that judgment on their genuineness belongs to those who lead the Church, to test all things and hold fast to what is good.

further_reading.title: The Orthodox Faith, Volume IV (Spirituality), Prayer, Fasting and Almsgiving: Prayer in the Spirit
further_reading.says: It treats speaking in tongues as a gift Paul describes and that some believers have in our time, finds no evidence that the saints prayed in tongues or that it was part of the church's liturgy, and says such prayer needs interpretation and order.

further_reading.title: Commission on Theology and Church Relations, The Charismatic Movement and Lutheran Theology (1972), conclusions
further_reading.says: It states that God does not necessarily give his church in all ages the same special gifts, rejects making tongues the primary or indispensable sign of baptism in the Spirit and a second work of the Spirit beyond conversion, and holds that the Word and sacraments are the means of grace.

further_reading.title: Smalcald Articles, Part III, Article VIII (Of Confession)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God grants his Spirit or grace to no one except through or with the preceding outward Word, and speaks against those who claim the Spirit without and before the Word.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 1 (Of the Holy Scripture), paragraph 1
further_reading.says: It ends paragraph 1 by saying that the former ways of God's revealing his will to his people have now ceased; it does not name tongues.

further_reading.title: Report of the Committee on the Baptism and Gifts of the Holy Spirit (45th General Assembly, 1978)
further_reading.says: The report concludes that prophecy and tongues ceased with the close of the apostolic age, while holding that God's power to heal in answer to prayer continues; the page notes that General Assembly reports are not constitutional documents.

further_reading.title: Pastoral Letter Concerning the Experience of the Holy Spirit in the Church Today (General Assembly)
further_reading.says: The letter rejects tongues as a means of receiving new revelation and as an essential sign of Spirit baptism, calls any practice that causes dissension in the body of Christ contrary to the purpose of the Spirit's gifts, and urges forbearance; it does not forbid tongues outright.

further_reading.title: Position statement on Pentecostalism
further_reading.says: It says Christ distributes his gifts when and where he wills, that genuine gifts may be exercised provided all things are done for edification and in good order, that gifts must be confirmed by the fruit of the Spirit, and that a believer receives baptism in the Spirit at conversion.

further_reading.title: To Be a Christian: An Anglican Catechism (2019), question 90
further_reading.says: It lists other languages (tongues) and the interpretation of other languages among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and says the Spirit distributes gifts to individuals as he wills for the sake of the Body of Christ.

further_reading.title: Book of Resolutions: Guidelines: The UMC and the Charismatic Movement (adopted 2008, readopted 2016 and 2024)
further_reading.says: It calls on the church to be aware of and respond to manifestations of the Holy Spirit today, describes the charismatic movement as stressing Spirit baptism without making tongues its initial evidence, and says that when tongues are spoken in a group there must be interpretation to ensure proper order.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 89, The More Excellent Way, paragraph 2
further_reading.says: Wesley gives as the cause of the extraordinary gifts becoming rare that the love of many Christians grew cold, and rejects the account that they were no longer needed.

further_reading.body: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches
further_reading.title: Articles of Faith, Article III (The Holy Spirit)
further_reading.says: It says the sign and revelatory gifts of the Holy Spirit have fulfilled their purpose and are not applicable to the work of the Holy Spirit today; it does not name tongues.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 1 (Of the Holy Scriptures), paragraph 1
further_reading.says: It ends paragraph 1 by saying that the former ways of God's revealing his will to his people have now ceased; it does not name tongues.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article II (God), section C (God the Holy Spirit)
further_reading.says: It says the Spirit bestows the spiritual gifts by which believers serve God through his church; it does not mention tongues or say whether the gifts continue.

further_reading.title: Statement of Fundamental Truths, 7 (The Baptism in the Holy Spirit) and 8 (The Initial Physical Evidence)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the baptism in the Holy Spirit is distinct from and subsequent to the new birth, and that it is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance.

further_reading.title: A. Reuben Hartwick, Speaking in Tongues: The Initial Physical Evidence of the Baptism in the Holy Spirit (a resource on the Assemblies of God site)
further_reading.says: It prints Fundamental Truths 7 and 8, including the sentence that tongues as initial evidence are the same in essence as the gift of tongues of 1 Corinthians 12 but different in purpose and use.

further_reading.title: Church of God Declaration of Faith
further_reading.says: It states belief in speaking with other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance, as the initial evidence of the baptism with the Holy Ghost, which it places after a clean heart.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 3 (Holy Spirit), commentary
further_reading.says: It does not mention tongues; it says the church builds itself up by the gifts of the Spirit given to each member, that the Spirit of God is not silent in the present, and that what is claimed is tested in the community of faith by the norm provided in Christ through the Scriptures.

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked. Agreed: Acts 2:4; 1 Cor 12:7; 1 Cor 13:2; 1 Cor 14:26 (second sentence). Reading 1: Acts 2:39 (full verse, closing curly quote dropped; the server's hyphen kept); Acts 10:46 (first sentence); Acts 19:6; 1 Cor 13:1 (first clause); 14:2; 14:5 (first clause, to 'tongues'); 14:14; 14:39. Reading 2: Acts 2:6 (clause from 'each one'); Acts 10:45; Acts 19:6; 1 Cor 12:28; 13:8 (clauses from 'where there are prophecies'); 13:10; 14:21 (the quoted saying, curly quotes dropped); 14:22 (first sentence). Reading 3: 12:11; 12:30; 14:19 (clause from 'in the church'); 14:27; 14:28 (clause from 'if there is no interpreter'; 'only' is the verse's own); 14:33 (hyphen kept); 14:39; 14:40 (clause from 'everything'). Acts 2:38, 2:17, 1 Cor 12:13, 14:4, 14:10-11, 14:12 and Isa 28:11 were read against the server too, because the answers and terms refer to them; Acts 2:38 'the gift of the Holy Spirit', 1 Cor 12:13 'in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body', 14:4 'edifies himself', and Isa 28:11 'with mocking lips and foreign tongues' (which differs in wording from Paul's quotation at 14:21; the note in reading 2 says the words 'stand in Isaiah 28:11-12', and a reviewer may want to say 'stand near' or 'are taken from'). ORDER: by when each reading was articulated, as I read the history. First, the gifts continue: the reading of the early church's experience, taking its present organised form with the Pentecostal movement of the 1900s. Second, the sign gifts ended: argued in the Reformation era and after against claims of continuing miracles, and set out as a position in the 1800s. Third, open but cautious: common in the twentieth century, after the Charismatic renewal reached the older churches. This is by date of articulation and not by size or preference, and a reviewer can reorder. THREE READINGS, AND WHERE THE LANGUAGE QUESTION IS: the brief names 'human languages or another speech' as a fourth item. It runs across the three readings (a Pentecostal may hold either answer, so may a cessationist-leaning reader, though most hold the first), so I put it in each reading's summary and answers, and in the terms (glossolalia and xenolalia), and not in a reading of its own, which would have needed a held_by that no tradition owns. Reviewers who want it as its own reading can ask for it; the verses would be Acts 2:6 and 2:8, 1 Cor 13:1, 14:2, 14:10-11. PASSAGES: eight in each reading. Acts 19:6 and 1 Cor 14:39 are cited by two readings, with different notes, because both sides cite them first. HELD_BY: assignments are approximate and the summaries say where members differ. I gave reading 1 to Pentecostal / Charismatic only, and named Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Reformed and Baptist members as holding it in part in its summary. I left Lutheran out of readings 2 and 3 and Eastern Orthodox out of all three because I could not state either tradition's position on this question fairly in one line; a Lutheran and an Orthodox reviewer should say where their tradition belongs and the card can be amended. The 'charism' term is given as the Catholic word only; an Orthodox reviewer should say whether it needs an Orthodox note. Nothing names a person, scholar, leader or movement's founder. WORDS: I checked the summaries, answers and notes for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely' and removed or avoided them; they appear only inside quotes (the verse's own words). 'Open but cautious' is the owner's phrase for the third reading; its holders may not use it as their own, and the label could be reworded. THE 1 CORINTHIANS 13:8 VERB: the site marks that the Berean's 'restrained' renders a Greek verb (paúō, 'to cease') different from the one said of prophecies and knowledge (katargeō). Reading 2 takes the difference as meaning something and reading 1 takes it as variation in wording; both are stated as holders' readings. I did not say which is right and did not say the Berean's word is wrong. LEFT OUT: (a) Acts 2:17 and 2:38 (the last days, the gift of the Spirit), 1 Cor 14:18 (Paul speaks in tongues more than all), 14:4, 14:10-11 and 14:12, kept in answers or terms for the count of eight; (b) passages outside the scope the owner gave: Mark 16:17 (in the longer ending of Mark, which the site marks, so I left it alone), Romans 8:26, Ephesians 2:20, Hebrews 2:3-4, 2 Corinthians 12:12, Jude 20; the cessationist reading in particular cites Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3-4 first, and a reviewer from that side may ask to widen the scope to include them; (c) women in the assembly (1 Cor 14:34-35), which is a different question; (d) the rule of 14:29-33 on weighing prophecy, because the card is about tongues; (e) the many claims about history after the apostles, kept out because the card speaks about the text. REVIEWERS: Catholic: the third reading's mention of 'those who lead it' states the teaching on testing the charisms in general terms, and a Catholic reviewer should confirm; the Catholic Charismatic Renewal is named only as 'charismatic renewal movements within their churches' in reading 1. Pentecostal and young African American believer: I kept Pentecostal practice from reading as emotional excess or as fringe, stated its terms in its own words (prayer language, baptism in the Holy Spirit, initial evidence) and noted that the family itself differs on initial evidence. Rabbi: the Isaiah 28 passage behind 1 Cor 14:21 is addressed to Isaiah's people and Paul introduces it as 'the Law', his name for the scriptures of Israel; the note says so and says nothing about what it means for Israel today. A rabbi should say whether 'Isaiah's own people' and 'a people who do not listen' need softening. Secular scholar: I used the scholars' terms (glossolalia, xenolalia) as terms, and the card does not compare tongues with ecstatic speech in other religions, which falls outside the question the owner set. Biblical-theology teacher: 1 Cor 12-14 is read as one argument on gifts and love (the agreed block uses 12:7, 13:2 and 14:26 for that). UNRESOLVED: whether the language question needs a reading of its own; the Lutheran and Orthodox placement; whether 'stand in Isaiah 28:11-12' in reading 2 should say 'are taken from'; and the Catholic wording.
